correctness.rationale: For prime \(p\ge5\), evenness of \(a_{2p-1}\) restricts \(b_{2p}\) to \(1\) or \(p\). If \(b_{2p}=1\), primality of \(p\) makes it divide a single factor \(1+b_k\); the bound \(1+b_k\le2p\) leaves only \(b_k=p-1\) or \(2p-1\). Divisibility \(b_k\mid k\), parity of earlier \(a_n\), and \(8\mid a_n\) for \(n\ge6\) exclude both possible indices for \(b_k=p-1\), forcing \(k=2p-1\). The reverse implication follows because \(1+b_{2p-1}=2p\). No finite experiment is used in the infinite proof.

value.rationale: The theorem identifies a natural structural mechanism in the exact recurrence studied by the recent source: forced-one increments on the canonical semiprime slice \(2p\) are controlled by one adjacent maximal increment. This both localizes the unresolved conjectural input and shows that the original \(K=1\) sequence already has a prime-pair detector, paralleling but not duplicating the source's motivation for introducing \(K=2\). The fact is infinite, exact, and explanatory rather than a finite census or a renamed textbook deduction.
